1 Introduction

Heteroatom doping is a pivotal strategy in materials science, significantly influencing the electronic, optical, and structural properties of materials [1−6]. By introducing atoms into a host lattice, researchers can tailor the material’s characteristics to meet specific technological needs [7−9]. This process allows for the fine-tuning of electronic band structures, enhancing conductivity, or modifying optical absorption properties, thereby expanding the material’s applicability in various fields such as semiconductors, catalysts, spintronics, and sensors. The ability to manipulate these properties through heteroatom doping underscores its importance in developing advanced materials with customized functionalities.

2 Experimental

2.2 Sample characterization

STM and STS measurements were performed at 4.2 K using a Scienta Omicron LT-STM/STS system under an ultra-high vacuum condition with a base pressure better than 1.0 × 10−10 mbar. A constant current mode was used during the STM scanning with an electrochemically etched W tip. The Nanotec Electronica WSxM software was used to process the STM images [25]. A lock-in technique was used with a modulation voltage of 5 mV and at a frequency of 599 Hz during the STS measurements.

2.3 Theoretical calculation

We considered a unit cell with a 3 × 3 monolayer AgTe on a 3-layer thick Ag(111) substrate with a vacuum distance of 15 Å, and the bottom two layers of the Ag(111) substrate were fixed. This work was performed in the Vienna ab-initio simulation package (VASP) [26] using first principles based on density functional theory (DFT). The exchange–correlation interactions were described using the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) [27], and Grimme’s DFT-D3 [28] method was applied to account for weak van der Waals interactions. In all calculations, a slab model measuring 14.95 Å × 14.95 Å × 25.00 Å and containing 99 atoms was employed. The model featured a 3 × 3 monolayer AgTe on a three-layer Ag(111) substrate, with the bottom two layers of the Ag(111) substrate fixed. The plane wave cutoff energy was set to 400 eV in all calculations. During structural optimization and self-consistency, 1 × 1 × 1 regular sampling was performed in the Brillouin zone and all atoms were allowed to relax until all forces and the total energy tolerance were below 0.02 eV·Å−1 and 10−4 eV. The band structure was calculated by including spin-orbit coupling (SOC). The Rashba parameters Δ were calculated using the formula [29]: Δ=2E0k0, where E0 and k0 values for the AgSexTe1−x bands are provided in Table S1 in the Electronic Supplementary Material (ESM).

3 Results and discussion

The flowchart for the whole sample preparation process is illustrated in Fig. 1(a). Initially, a large-area, high-quality AgTe monolayer was prepared by a one-step direct tellurization of the Ag(111) substrate, which had been clearly demonstrated in our previously work [14]. Subsequently, a small quantity of selenium atoms was deposited onto the clean, large-area and high-quality AgTe monolayer. After that, the sample was annealed to 473 K. Through this procedure, the Se atoms substituted the Te atoms in the AgTe monolayer, thus yielding a Se-doped AgTe (AgSexTe1−x) monolayer. Figure 1(b) presents an atomic-resolution STM image of the pristine AgTe monolayer grown on the Ag(111) substrate. The image exhibits a defect-free surface featuring a honeycomb lattice structure. In our previously published paper [14], joint experimental–computational analysis shows that the electronic state intensity of Te atoms is greater than that of Ag atoms in AgTe monolayers. The brighter contrast in STM images therefore directly corresponds to Te atoms.

DFT calculations were conducted on the AgSexTe1−x monolayer with varying concentrations of Se (0 ≤ x ≤ 1). To computationally simulate the Rashba effect in AgSexTe1−x monolayers with varying Se concentrations, we calculated the projected band structures for AgTe, AgTe0.67Se0.33, AgTe0.33Se0.67, and AgSe as representative cases. The Rashba parameters of the β and γ bands were quantitatively analyzed. The atomic configurations of these four models are illustrated in Fig. S1 in the ESM. Figure 4(a) illustrates three distinct energy bands of AgTe monolayer, labeled as α, β, and γ. The α and β bands within the valence band primarily originate from contributions of the Te pxy orbital, while the γ band is predominantly derived from the hybridization of the Ag s orbital and the Te pz orbital. The energy separation between α and β is 0.3 eV, which is in line with the experimental value of 0.31 eV reported in prior studies [18]. It is worth noting that the orbital splitting of the β and γ bands exhibits a linear dependence on k||, whereas the orbital splitting of the α band follows a cubic relationship with k||, as shown in Fig. 4(b). The small spin splitting in the α band arises from higher-order contributions, with the Rashba term being negligible (Δα ≈ 0). The Rashba parameters of β and γ bands are Δβ = 0.92 eV·Å and Δγ = 0.87 eV·Å, respectively (Fig. S2 in the ESM), which is consistent with previous report [16].

4 Conclusions

In conclusion, our comprehensive investigation of Se substitution doping in monolayer AgSexTe1−x has yielded valuable insights into the modulation of Rashba splitting and the structural properties of 2D materials. Utilizing a combination of STM imaging and first-principles calculations, we have shown that Se doping can substantially modify the atomic structure and electronic properties of monolayer AgSexTe1−x. Notably, substituting Te atoms with Se atoms leads to a decrease in the Rashba parameter. This decrease is due to alterations in the in-plane potential gradient, which are caused by the difference in atomic radii between Te and Se. The ability to manipulate the Rashba effect through substitutional doping offers a promising route for shaping the electronic and structural characteristics of monolayer materials. Our results provide an effective approach to modulate the electronic properties of monolayer materials through substitutional doping. This strategy opens up new possibilities for tailoring the structural and electronic characteristics of monolayer materials to meet specific requirements in nanoelectronics and spintronics applications.

Abstract

Binary honeycomb monolayer AgTe are experimentally evident to possess notably Rashba effect. Effective modulation of Rashba splitting facilitates the application of monolayer AgTe in spintronic devices. Here, we systematically investigated the effects of Se atom substitution doping on the atomic structure and the magnitude of Rashba splitting within monolayer AgSexTe1−x on the Ag(111) substrate, utilizing scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) imaging and first-principles calculations. In the monolayer AgTe, Se atoms can easily substitute for the Te atoms, and they exhibit a more pronounced electronic state than Te atoms. Following the deposition of additional Se atoms and the subsequent annealing process, the proportion of Se atom substitution gradually increases. Once the value of x exceeds 0.33, domain boundaries appear within the AgSexTe1−x monolayer. The density functional theory (DFT) calculation results indicate that as the atomic radius decreases from Te to Se, the reduced nuclear Coulomb potential alters the surface geometry. As a result, this gives rise to changes in the in-plane potential gradient and a corresponding decline in the Rashba parameter. Our finding provides a new approach for modulating the atomic structure and Rashba splitting of monolayer AgTe, which paves the way for the utilization of monolayer AgTe in the fields of nanoelectronics and spintronics.
